question_type: Absolute difference of two 4-month sums (two commodity rows) from a two-block customs table (duties block, then values block) whose values-block header labels are OCR-offset from the data

opus_path.decision: Issue pinned to March 1941; table = 'Customs Duties and Taxes Collected, and Values of Dutiable and Taxable Imports, Estimated by Tariff Schedules'; the question's 'Internal Revenue collections' wording is loose; use the VALUES block (not duties) for rows 'Tobacco and manufactures' and 'Wool and manufactures'; months Feb-May 1940; thousands -> millions, 2 decimals.
grep for 'dutiable' in the March 1941 issue located the title and the values-block total row.

Read the whole table (both blocks) and noticed the values-block header has more labels than data cells, i.e. labels are offset by one or two columns; interpreted the numeric cells as [CY1939, CY1940, Jan40..Dec40, Jan41].
Verified the column mapping by checking that the 12 monthly 1940 cells sum exactly to the CY1940 cell for the Tobacco, Wool and Total rows.
Cross-issue check: the Feb-May 1940 value cells are identical in every 1940-41 printing, so no vintage risk.
Summed the four months per row in calc.py, took the absolute difference, converted thousands to millions.
Computed and rejected two alternatives: using the duties block, and trusting the offset header labels (which selects Mar-Jun).

opus_key_moves: Chose the values block over the duties block from the question's 'values' wording and used the same block for both rows.
Did not trust the OCR header labels; proved the month-to-column mapping with a months-sum-to-annual check on the rows actually used.
Extracted cells from the source lines in code rather than by eye.

first_divergence.what_glm_did: Mixed blocks and month windows in one difference: for tobacco it took the values-block row but mapped months by the offset header labels (so it summed Mar-Jun instead of Feb-May); for wool it took the DUTIES-block row (aligned header, Feb-May) because the values-block wool row was never on screen.
first_divergence.what_opus_did: Used the values block for both rows and fixed the month mapping by a months-sum-to-annual check (worklog.md:38-43).
first_divergence.why_glm_went_that_way: [18] states 'They ask values, so second table', then lists numbers without a visible column check. Its read windows ended at line 1709 ([15]) and at the values-block header line 1699 ([17]), so the values-block tobacco row (1706) was visible but the values-block wool row (1711) was not; the only 'Wool and manufactures' row it had seen was the duties-block one (1676). It trusted the values-block header labels, which are offset one column from the data.
first_divergence.consequence: Both operands wrong (tobacco shifted a month, wool from the wrong block); about 75% low.

secondary_errors.note: Fixed-size line windows (150-line helper cap) cut the table mid-block; it never re-read to reach the rest of the values block.
Arithmetic was scripted, but on hand-typed numbers, so the script could not catch the selection errors.

saw_correct_evidence.where: [15] output displayed the values-block tobacco row and [17] the values-block header; the values-block wool row was never displayed.

remedies.intervention: Table-block extractor: given a title or line, return the whole table (title to footnotes) as a grid per block, with header labels realigned when the label count differs from the data-cell count, and cells addressable as (block, row, column).
remedies.why: The none arm's 150-line windows cut the values block before the wool row and it then grabbed a same-named row from the other block; a whole-table grid removes both failure paths.

remedies.intervention: Same-source consistency check for multi-operand formulas: operands of one difference/ratio must come from the same block and the same column indices unless the question says otherwise.
remedies.why: Its two operands came from different blocks of the table, which a citation-level check flags directly.

remedies.intervention: Require cited extraction: numbers enter the computation only through a script that pulls them from cited file:line and column indices (no hand-typed literals), and the script prints the cited cells next to the header labels.
remedies.why: Its only script ([19]) summed hand-typed numbers, so the script could not detect that the numbers came from the wrong cells.

right_arms_note: No GLM arm was right. The none arm mixed the duties and values blocks (partial read window) and trusted the offset labels; the prompt and cards arms made the identical one-column slip on the wool row while reading tobacco correctly.
text_vs_mechanism: Needs a mechanism. The prompt arm had text saying not to eyeball flattened multi-panel tables and to compute in python, and eyeballed anyway; the cards arm obeyed its script card only for the arithmetic. A months-sum-to-annual check or a recompute-from-cited-cells check would have caught all three arms; an aligned-grid table tool would have prevented them.
notes: The two adapted arms produced the same wrong value, which points to a systematic model bias when reading rows under an offset header: it reads different rows of one block with different column alignments. Header offset is machine-detectable here (label count exceeds data-cell count by one). All three arms found the right table quickly despite the question's misleading 'Internal Revenue collections' wording, so the failure is purely at cell selection/extraction, the cheapest place to add a check.
